journey.note: Multiplier 8 from the parents' average age, 1/3 deduction, no future prospects, Rs 2,000 for loss of companionship. Date not stated.
Multiplier 11 from the parents' ages (54 and 53), 50% deduction, no future prospects. The High Court, the date and who appealed are not stated.

Connected appeal C.A. No. 178/2017 allowed to the extent of the recomputed table: multiplier 16 by the deceased's own age, 50% future prospects, 50% deduction, Rs 30,000 for loss of companionship; Rs 5,92,876 more, with 9% interest.

precedent.holding: When an unmarried person (a bachelor) dies in a motor accident, the multiplier is chosen by the age of the deceased, not the age of the parents or other dependents. A three-judge bench treated this as settled by Sube Singh, Munna Lal Jain, Reshma Kumari and Pranay Sethi and rejected the insurer's plea to use the dependents' ages.

extraction.title_anon: Salaried person, Rs 7,242 a month, state not stated (death)
extraction.family_summary: A salaried person earning Rs 7,242 a month died in a road accident. The tribunal awarded Rs 4,65,488 and the High Court Rs 4,79,972, both choosing the multiplier from the parents' ages. On 9 April 2019 the Supreme Court decided this appeal together with three related appeals. Following its ruling in the lead case, it used the deceased's own age (multiplier 16), added 50% future prospects and raised the award to Rs 10,72,848 with 9% interest. The earlier dates are not given; the Supreme Court appeal was numbered in 2017.
what_mattered: The Supreme Court held that the multiplier follows the deceased's own age, not the parents' ages, which lifted it from 11 to 16.
Future prospects of 50% were added for the first time, and loss of companionship went up from Rs 2,000 to Rs 30,000.
The court heard the multiplier point even though the other side said it was not raised, because a ground in the appeal petition was wide enough to cover it.
